questions.question: Why can't you run ML inference on data encrypted with standard symmetric encryption (e.g., AES)?
options: Standard encryption requires decryption before any computation; the server sees plaintext during inference
AES keys are too short to protect ML model weights
Neural networks only work on floating-point numbers, which AES cannot encrypt
Standard encryption produces non-deterministic output, breaking gradient descent
questions.explanation: Standard encryption is not homomorphic: you must decrypt to compute, exposing plaintext to whoever runs the computation.

questions.question: In BFV, what is the role of the scaling factor Delta = round(q/t)?
options: It lifts the plaintext into the most-significant bits of Z_q so that small noise does not corrupt the message after rounding
It compresses the ciphertext to save bandwidth
It is used as the secret key during decryption
It sets the maximum number of homomorphic multiplications allowed
questions.explanation: Delta separates message bits from noise bits: the plaintext sits at the top of Z_q, and noise lives in the low-order bits below Delta/2.

questions.question: After encrypting m under BFV, decryption computes v = c0 + <c1, s> mod q. What does v contain?
options: encode(m) plus accumulated noise from encryption
The raw message m with no noise
The secret key s XORed with the message
A hash of m that requires a lookup table to invert
questions.explanation: v = Delta*m + noise. As long as |noise| < Delta/2, rounding v/Delta recovers m exactly.

questions.question: Why does homo_scalar_mul(enc(m), w) increase the noise in the ciphertext?
options: Both ciphertext components are multiplied by w, so the embedded noise term is also scaled by w
The operation re-encrypts with fresh noise of magnitude w
Scalar multiplication modifies the secret key, adding key-dependent noise
It does not increase noise; only ciphertext-ciphertext multiplication does
questions.explanation: Multiplying (c0, c1) by w scales all components including the noise: new_noise = w * old_noise.

questions.question: In this toy scheme, what happens when the total accumulated noise exceeds q/(2t)?
options: The rounding step in decryption picks the wrong multiple of Delta, producing an incorrect plaintext
The ciphertext becomes non-invertible and cannot be decrypted
The scheme raises a ValueError automatically to signal budget exhaustion
The noise wraps around mod q and cancels, giving a correct result
questions.explanation: Decryption is exact rounding: if noise >= Delta/2 = q/(2t), the nearest-multiple-of-Delta is wrong and m is corrupted.

questions.question: The server evaluates sum_i(w_i * enc(x_i)) + enc(bias) and returns an encrypted score. What does the server learn about x_i or the final prediction?
options: Nothing — all values remain encrypted throughout; only the client with the secret key can decrypt
The server learns the feature values because it must decode them to apply the weights
The server learns the prediction class because it compares the encrypted score to the threshold
The server learns the bias because it encrypts it itself using the public key
questions.explanation: Homomorphic evaluation is done entirely in ciphertext space. The server sees only ciphertexts and public parameters — no plaintext is ever revealed.

questions.question: Which of these is the main reason real FHE inference uses CKKS instead of BFV?
options: CKKS supports approximate real-valued arithmetic natively, which matches the floating-point weights and activations in neural networks
CKKS has a smaller ciphertext modulus and therefore runs faster on all hardware
BFV cannot perform addition homomorphically; only CKKS supports it
CKKS eliminates noise entirely, making decryption always exact
questions.explanation: Neural networks use real-valued arithmetic; BFV works over integers mod t. CKKS encodes approximate real numbers and tolerates small rounding errors, making it a natural fit for ML.

questions.question: You want to add a sixth feature with weight 5000 to this linear model. The current noise budget headroom is ~2^31. A fresh ciphertext has noise ~B=8. Is this safe?
options: No — homo_scalar_mul by 5000 scales the noise to 5000*8 = 40000 per term; adding six such terms gives ~240000, still well within 2^31, so it is actually safe
No — a weight of 5000 immediately exhausts the noise budget regardless of B
Yes — scalar multiplication never affects noise budget
Yes — only ciphertext-ciphertext multiplication affects the budget; scalar ops are free
questions.explanation: Noise after one scalar-mul is |w|*B = 5000*8 = 40000. Summing six terms: ~240000. Budget is ~2^31 ≈ 2,000,000,000. The operation is safe.
